Vital signs (heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), SpO2, blood pressure) were also collected at 1 min intervals (Philips Monitoring, Amsterdam, The Netherlands/Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA). HR and RR were averaged over the time blocks, the per cent difference between baseline and the procedure was determined and the value was then subcategorised by a score of 0-2 as shown in table 1.

Sensor recordings were performed using flexible wireless biosensors. The sensor devices were constructed (online supplemental material) and contained an accelerometer and gyroscope to detect three-dimensional position data, allowing movements to be translated to vital signs including HR, RR and vocalisations. Two sensors were adhered to each infant's chest and the dorsal aspect of a foot using a hydrogel adhesive and Masimo NEO Adhesive tape (Irvine, California, USA) (figure 1). A sensor recording was performed and included the time blocks of baseline and procedure. The sensor data were recorded locally to the device, then wirelessly transmitted using the Discovery RA app Sibel (Chicago, Illinois, USA) onto a research iOS device, and transferred for data storage and analyses in .shrd and .xlxs formats.

Example of waveform data from a chest and limb sensor recording over nearly 3000 s. The recording is scored as if there is an ongoing mildly painful procedure to provide examples of the application of the sensor pain score criteria. There are three subcategories represented: crying/irritability by vocal frequency (Hz), behaviour state/lower extremity movement and vital sign changes. The data are numerically scored to provide examples of the applied criterion (0-1-2). Diff. Temp, differential temperature; HR, heart rate; RR, respiratory rate.

The sensor-derived data by infant were processed as discrete measures per second in CVS format and was transformed into waveforms and graphics in a jpeg file, as shown in figure 1. Mean HR and RR were calculated during the time blocks; the per cent difference between the two was determined and the change in values was subcategorised as a score of 0-2 (table 1).
The start/stop times of the sensor recording were also documented to ensure they aligned with the video recordings.
Data scoring

Scorers included four paediatric neonatologists with clinical expertise and four non-clinicians with paediatric research experience. All scorers received NPASS training using the standardised approach adopted in the local NICU, which has been validated for internal consistency. The eight scorers were divided into two groups (group 1, n=2 and group 2, n=6). The first group provided feedback on the CSPS training that mirrored NPASS training and included a review of the criteria with visual examples of scored waveforms (not part of the testing set) and provided clinical explanations. The feedback from the first group focused on the instructional training materials, while the CSPS criteria remained consistent between scorer groups. All NPASS and CSPS training materials were available as a reference during scoring. Scorers independently scored the recordings at baseline and the procedure, applying NPASS criteria to the video recordings and CSPS criteria to the sensor recordings (table 1).
The sensor recordings were assessed and scored using two approaches: (1) CSPS and (2) ASPS (table 1).

The CSPS criterion was derived from NPASS. Crying and irritability, behaviour state with movement and vital sign changes were chosen measures to record with the sensor and transform into waveform data for visualisation and scoring. Like NPASS, CSPS has subcategories, each corresponding with a score of 0-2, and is scaled by summing the subcategories for a total score of 0-6; 0 being the absence of pain and 6 being a moderate level of pain. A maximum score of 6 would capture a response to a procedure such as a heel lance. The subcategories of CSPS were defined by literature review, previous sensor research and expert opinion from nursing, field researchers, neonatologists and bioengineers (table 1). An example of an assessment using CSPS is illustrated in figure 1. Of note, the CSPS differs from the NPASS assessment in that it does not include facial expression, as this can be subjective and involve identifiable patient data, nor infant tone, since it can be subjective even with handling.

The ASPS criterion was formulated using the CSPS criteria (table 1). The CVS data were analysed using a semi-automated decision tree model with branching logic and artificial intelligence with support vector regression learning. For the crying and irritability subcategory, the data were sampled over a 3 s, 300-sample window. The frequency outcome was labelled '0' for windows with averages <50 Hz: '1' for those with a frequency SD under 30 Hz signifying prolonged crying and '2' for windows that have max frequency exceeding 450 Hz. For the behaviour state subcategory, a machine learning model was initially trained to classify the data by manually scoring results against the criteria in table 1. A 60 s rolling window was used with a 50% overlap, and each window was classified into a score of 0, 1 or 2. The support vector machine model was trained to follow criteria listed in table 1. Largely, 0 was assigned to windows most often without movement, label 1 to windows with movement most often ranging from 0.1 to 0.2 g (gravitational acceleration constant) and level 2 to movement most often exceeding 0.2 g. The vital sign subcategory score was derived from the per cent difference in HR and RR during the laboratory draw compared with the baseline measures.

Video recordings of infants at baseline and during the procedure were scored using the NPASS criteria (table 1). If consent to video record was not obtained, the time blocks were scored at bedside by a clinician expert in real-time using the NPASS criteria.
Statistical analyses
Cohort characteristics were analysed using descriptive statistics and compared using chi2 analysis.

Sensor and video recordings were scored using the CSPS, ASPS and NPASS, with both subcategory and total scores assessed at baseline and during the phlebotomy procedure. The CSPS and NPASS results were examined for inter-rater reliability with ICC estimates and 95% CIs based on a mean-rating (k=6), consistency, two-way random-effects modelling by total score as well as Cronbach's alpha for internal consistency. The median total score and median subcategory scores of the CSPS and ASPS were compared with NPASS scores using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and overall with the Kruskal-Wallis test. Bland-Altman plots were made to illustrate systematic differences between the measurements and outliers.
Results

Forty infants were consented for study enrolment and 36 were available for recordings during the phlebotomy procedure. Thirty-two infants were included in the analyses with CSPS, ASPS and NPASS scores available (one excluded for technical issues with the sensor recording and three with video recording). Two infants had bedside NPASS assessments performed.

The patient demographic and recording details are described in table 2. Of the 32 infants in the cohort, 12 were female (20 male) with more than six race and ethnicities (not Hispanic white n=15, black or African-American n=5, Hispanic white n=4, Hispanic, Latino or Spanish origin 'none of the above' n=3, not Hispanic, Latino or Spanish origin 'none of the above' n=3, Asian or Asian Indian n=2). The admitting diagnosis was most often prematurity (n=26), followed by respiratory distress (n=2), desaturations (n=2), hypoglycaemia (n=1) and low birth weight (n=1).

The median CSPS and ASPS scores were not significantly different from NPASS scores during the procedure (CSPS: z=-0.07, p=0.95; ASPS: z=-0.28, p=0.56), indicating the scores were comparable. The Bland-Altman plots (figure 2) show close agreement between NPASS and CSPS (mean difference -0.20; limits of agreement of -1.9 to 1.4) and between NPASS and ASPS (mean difference 0.22; limits of agreement of -1.6 to 2.0). The median CSPS and ASPS scores during the procedure were also statistically similar (z-score 0.08; p=0.94). The Bland-Altman plot between CSPS and ASPS scores (figure 2) had close agreement, with a mean difference of -0.016 and limits of agreement of -1.27 to 1.30. Score differences across CSPS, ASPS and NPASS were evenly distributed around the line of mean difference within these limits, indicating consistent assessment of mild and moderate pain by the assessment tools (figure 2).

The dashed line represents the mean difference, and the grey box denotes the upper and lower limits of agreement. Size of the data points proportionally represents the number of patients with the same assigned scores.

By criteria subcategory, CSPS and NPASS median scores during the procedure were different for cry and irritability (CSPS 0 (Q1 0, Q3 2; NPASS 0 (0, 0.5); z-score 2.5; p=0.01) and similar for behaviour state (z-score 1.2; p=0.22) and vital signs (z-score 0.01; p=1.0). By criteria subcategory, ASPS and NPASS procedure scores were similar (crying and irritability z-score 1.09, p=0.27; behaviour state z-score 1.65, p=0.10; vital signs z-score 0.01, p=1.0). By subcategory score, ASPS scores were statistically similar to the CSPS scores in crying and irritability, behaviour state and vital signs (z-score 0.94; p=0.35; z-score 0.69; p=0.49; z-score 0.01; p=1.0).
Discussion

This study confirmed the successful application of a wireless, wearable, non-invasive device to monitor key behavioural and autonomic features of pain in preterm and term infants, capturing continuous changes in vocalisations, movement and vital signs during an acute nociceptive stimulus.

We applied CSPS and ASPS, NPASS-derived criteria, to distinguish pain from rest and quantify mild to moderate discomfort. The scored features of sensor recordings using CSPS and ASPS were determined to be statistically similar to one another and the NPASS score, a valid and reliable recommended infant pain assessment tool for use with acute pain. The pain scores by CSPS were more reliable than NPASS scores for those with less clinical expertise, as determined by higher inter-rater reliability. With the application of ASPS, the computerised, rule-based voting function provided an additional objective option for continuous pain monitoring in infants.

Our results are consistent with prior systematic reviews of infant pain assessment. A recent meta-review on infant pain assessment across 36 current pain scales (NPASS not included) reported that most available scales are focused on categorising acute pain using multiple variables, as was the focus of our study. Comparing previous systematic reviews, the authors found Face, Legs, Activity, Cry and Consolability (FLACC) and COMFORT were most frequently recommended for general infant pain assessments, although the reviews were heterogenous, making it difficult to recommend a single tool. The IRR and measures of validity for FLACC and COMFORT were reported to be high in some, but not all reviews. A systematic review on NPASS reported the tool to have good to excellent reliability and validity for infants of all GAs in assessing acute pain (ICC=0.93-0.99 and internal consistency (alpha)=0.837-0.971). In our study, ICC and internal consistency of CSPS were excellent and comparable to the NPASS measures of validity and reliability, and with significantly similar median scores to ASPS.

Beyond validity, our study addressed usability and clinical utility. While limited data exist for other infant pain assessment tools, our work contributes a modernised method of continuous monitoring while demonstrating ease of use, similar to a pulse-oximeter. Although the physiological data capture is comparable with other wearable biosensor studies analysing pain, particularly in adult medicine, the sensor used here is uniquely small and able to capture sensitive vocalisations and behavioural data in a non-cumbersome manner. Equally important, our study also demonstrated clinical utility. CSPS and ASPS showed versatility compared with other tools that require a highly trained bedside assessor. Although structured training was provided, non-clinicians achieved high inter-rater reliability using CSPS. This suggests that interpretation does not require advanced paediatric expertise. While the system involves reading waveform data, the reliability achieved by non-clinicians indicates that it may in fact be simpler to apply than bedside NPASS scoring. This supports the potential for broader applicability with streamlined training materials, similar to existing clinical pain scales. Furthermore, as integration with automated aids such as ASPS advances, and as sensor-based monitoring becomes more commonplace in NICUs, barriers related to training and waveform interpretation are likely to diminish, further enhancing generalisability and ease of clinical use.

Notably, CSPS and ASPS were designed to provide objective measures that allow for accurate and rapid patient assessment while reducing interpreter bias, variation in scoring and interval limitations. The most prominently used infant assessments for acute pain are based on subjective observations, such as with NPASS, Premature Infant Pain Profile-Revised, Neonatal Facial Coding System and Neonatal Infant Pain Scale. Like the objective measures of CSPS and ASPS, PRAMS and PainCheck Infant are contemporary semi-automated pain assessment tools that measure changes in infant facial expressions for classification of pain. By contrast, biosensor-based systems such as ours offer objective pain assessment through waveform data or automated algorithms, with additional advantages of patient mobility, reduced reliance on identifiable patient data and lower storage/computing costs. As objective tools, CSPS and ASPS are important for diagnosing infant pain and may help balance the risks of both overtreatment and undertreatment, which carry long-term neurodevelopmental risk in this vulnerable population.

Although encouraging, these results must be interpreted considering several limitations. First, the ASPS algorithm could be refined further, since the ASPS vocalisation subcategory had higher scores than CSPS and NPASS (eg, labelled '2', rather than a '1'). With additional subjects and data, more sensitive rules can be used in ASPS such as including a duration of a defined frequency that meets a score. Second, additional sensor features such as more detailed electrocardiography and electromyography may provide more detailed diagnostic information. Lastly, the cohort was representative of a diverse, populous US. city, and CSPS and ASPS diagnosed pain in each race and/or ethnicity group within the cohort, but underpowered for any defined associations. Likewise, as a single-centre study, results may not fully reflect practice across other NICU settings. While not excluded from the study, the use of sensors was not explored in infants with hypotonia and airway differences such as vocal cord anomalies and intubations, which may limit sensitivity where movement or vocalisations are varied.

Future research should focus on validating CSPS and ASPS in larger and more diverse infant populations, including younger preterm infants, and across different NICU settings. These studies will be important to confirm generalisability and to further establish the reliability of sensor-based pain assessment in clinical practice. In the long term, integration of ASPS into routine NICU monitoring could provide continuous, objective pain scores that support clinical judgement, alerting staff to changes in infant comfort.
Conclusions

This study demonstrated the feasibility of continuous wireless biosensor monitoring with applied diagnostics in the NICU. Both CSPS and ASPS aligned closely with NPASS scores and showed excellent reliability, while capturing infant vocalisations, behaviours and vital signs to objectively assess for mild to moderate acute pain in late preterm and term infants. These findings provide initial validation of biosensor-based approaches to infant pain assessment, supporting further research in larger and more diverse cohorts to confirm the validity and reliability of CSPS and ASPS.

passages.text: Systematic review of clinical outcomes from the implementation of hospital-based antimicrobial stewardship programs in India
ABSTRACT

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing concern that can compromise clinical outcomes as well as increase the significant economic stress on healthcare systems. Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) have demonstrated promising results in improving treatment outcomes and reducing costs worldwide. However, the effectiveness of ASP in Indian hospital settings remains underexplored. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of implementing ASP in Indian hospital settings. Literature search was carried out in electronic databases such as PubMed, Clinical Trials Registry-India, Clinicaltrials.gov, and Google Scholar from January 2015 till April 2025 to identify published studies that explored the clinical outcomes in Indian hospital-based settings that implemented ASP. Studies that assessed at least one of the following outcomes:AMR pattern, infection rate, mortality rate, prescription pattern, costs, or barriers/challenges in ASP implementation:were eligible for screening. Two independent reviewers screened the articles for eligibility, with discrepancies resolved through discussion with a third reviewer. Out of the 1732 studies screened, 11 studies were found eligible for inclusion. Those studies were conducted in different Indian states. Each study implemented different ASP practices, including infection control, audit and feedback, and customized training. Most of the studies evaluated demonstrated improvements such as a reduction in inappropriate prescriptions, lower antimicrobial resistance rates, decreased infection and mortality rates, and reduced costs following the implementation of ASP. Despite the benefits, implementation challenges remain. This review highlights the need for strict ASP implementation and monitoring in Indian hospitals to combat AMR.
Introduction
Burden of AMR globally and in India

A ntimicrobial agents, including antibiotics, antivirals, antifungals, and antiparasitics, form the cornerstone of modern medicine, enabling the treatment of a wide range of infectious diseases. However, the efficacy of these life-saving therapies is increasingly undermined by the escalating threat of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a global health concern in countries across all income levels.

Globally, India was the largest consumer of antibiotics for human health in 2010. The misuse or overuse of antibiotics often arises due to inappropriate prescription, self-medication, and incomplete treatment courses. A study reported that the total defined daily dose (DDD) of antibiotics consumed in 2019 was 5071 million, which is equivalent to 10.4 DDD per 1000 people per day. While the per-capita private-sector antibiotic consumption rate in India is relatively low when compared to many countries, it is alarming that a large volume of broad-spectrum antibiotics is still being consumed, even though they should be used only when clinically indicated. This improper usage of antimicrobials can result in AMR, increased costs, and poor patient outcomes. Indian hospital studies show that 60-70% of inpatients receive antimicrobials, with 30-50% prescribed inappropriately. Resistance is high, including >50% carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae in ICUs and widespread fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli, underscoring the urgent need for stewardship in Indian hospitals.
Link between AMR and clinical/economic outcomes

AMR not only compromises clinical outcomes but also imposes a significant economic burden due to prolonged hospital stays, increased healthcare costs, and higher mortality rates. Alarmingly, in 2019 alone, AMR was responsible for approximately 297,000 deaths in India:surpassing the mortality rates associated with neonatal and maternal conditions, diabetes, kidney diseases, enteric infections, respiratory illnesses, tuberculosis, and even neoplasms. If left unaddressed, AMR could result in catastrophic outcomes for India, where it was already responsible for approximately 297,000 deaths in 2019, with projections indicating a significant rise in mortality burden in the coming decades.

The link between AMR and adverse clinical outcomes is well established. Inappropriate, delayed, or suboptimal antimicrobial therapy is the main cause of increase in mortality, duration of hospitalization, and the total healthcare cost. The rising incidence of multidrug-resistant organism infections, particularly among patients in the intensive care unit who acquire healthcare-associated infections, is becoming a critical safety concern.
Antimicrobial stewardship programs: Concept and benefits

To mitigate resistant pathogens, a multifaceted approach ensuring rational antimicrobial use is needed. Hence, implementing an antimicrobial stewardship program (ASP) is beneficial. An ASP is a multidisciplinary program that improves prescribing to optimize outcomes while minimizing toxicity, pathogen selection, and resistance. With rising drug resistance, ASP is essential to optimize existing drugs. Effective ASPs ensure appropriate selection, dosing, duration, and route, alongside infection control, reducing resistant microorganisms. They have shown reductions in resistance, mortality, and costs, with antimicrobial use and costs decreasing by 22-36%. However, challenges include behavior change among patients and professionals and monitoring compliance. Additionally, the international pipeline of antibiotics has continued to be essentially stagnant, with nothing really new classes emerging in the past 10 years. This innovation deficit implies that our current antimicrobials are our most precious asset. In this light, the application of ASPs is even more important since they promote rational use of available drugs, extend their usability, and assist in maintaining treatment alternatives for generations to come.

passages.text: Challenges and barriers in India

Although ASP is recognized as a key strategy in India, there is a lack of a national-level antimicrobial stewardship plan. The barriers to the implementation of an effective ASP in low- and middle-income countries such as India include factors such as the lack of proper guidance and trained professionals, including pharmacists and infectious disease physicians. In India, there are model tertiary care centers like CMC Vellore and JIPMER Puducherry where ASPs have been implemented effectively, reflecting better prescription patterns and a decline in resistance. These instances prove that even as national implementation progresses, good models already exist and can be replicated across Indian hospitals.
Rationale for this systematic review

Given these challenges in implementing ASP, this systematic review aims to evaluate the effectiveness of ASP in India by assessing the clinical outcomes in hospitals that have already implemented them. By systematically reviewing the existing data on ASPs across different hospital settings, this review will help in understanding whether the implementation of ASPs is beneficial to tackle the growing concern of AMR in India.
Materials and Methods
Objectives

We aimed to evaluate the clinical outcomes, such as reduction in AMR, impact on infection rates and mortality, and changes in prescription practices, following the implementation of ASP in hospitals in India. We also aimed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of ASP implementation and the challenges associated with it. This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines (PRISMA statement given), and we also register our study in PROSPERO (CRD420251057499).
Eligibility criteria

This systematic review included qualitative and quantitative studies published in the English language that provide data on the aforementioned clinical outcomes following the implementation of ASP and were conducted in hospital-based settings in India. Completed studies published from 2015 to April 2025, including prospective and retrospective observational studies, surveillance studies, and cohort studies. Excluded were studies without relevant data and full texts, conducted in non-hospital-based settings, case reports, studies published before 2015, and non-English publications. We received ethical clearance to conduct this study from the concerned institutional ethics committee (PHH&RCLCREC/4418/2024).
Search strategy

We conducted a comprehensive literature search from January 2015 till April 2025 in databases such as PubMed, Clinical Trials Registry-India, Clinicaltrials.gov, and Google Scholar to identify studies that explored the clinical outcomes from the implementation of hospital-based ASP in India using the Medical Subject Heading (MeSH) terms "antimicrobial stewardship program," "antimicrobial resistance," "infection rates," "mortality," prescription practices," "India," and "hospital" in different combinations. Filters available in the relevant databases to include studies only between January 2015 and April 2025 were applied. This review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines.
Study selection

The full-text copies of the reported papers were downloaded for review after screening the abstract and title review. A total of 11 studies were included in the analysis after evaluation of the inclusion criteria. Data extracted from the identified studies included study design, setting, intervention, year of publication, region, study period, and findings.
Data extraction

Data extraction and synthesis were done independently by two authors. Any discrepancies were settled by consulting a third author, if needed. A spreadsheet designed specifically for this systematic review was used to remove duplicate records. No assumptions or simplifications of data were made to ensure accuracy and reproducibility. Study titles and abstracts were screened thoroughly, after which studies with full texts were reviewed to ensure the included studies were relevant and of high quality.
Quality assessment

To assess the methodological quality and risk of bias of the included studies, we utilized standardized critical appraisal tools appropriate for the study designs. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Quality Assessment Tools were used for observational cohort and cross-sectional studies, while the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools were applied for qualitative studies. These tools evaluate various domains such as study objectives, population selection, comparability of groups, outcome measures, and statistical methods.

Each study was independently assessed for quality by two reviewers. Disagreements in scoring or judgment were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Studies were categorized as having low, moderate, or high risk of bias based on predefined criteria. No studies were excluded solely on the basis of quality assessment; however, the quality ratings were considered during interpretation of the results and synthesis of evidence.
Data synthesis

The quality assessment ensured transparency and allowed us to identify potential limitations and biases in the body of evidence. The findings from this evaluation are summarized in a tabular format in the results section, providing an overview of the strengths and weaknesses of the studies included. Effect measures like risk ratio or mean difference were not applied due to heterogeneity in study designs, outcomes, and reporting. Many studies lacked variance data for pooled estimates. Instead, we used descriptive synthesis with raw percentages, before-after comparisons, and basic statistics (frequencies, proportions) to summarize outcomes across diverse study types without overstating precision.
Results
Study selection and characteristics

Overall, 1732 titles and abstracts were retrieved from various databases. Following duplicate records removal, 1520 records were eligible for screening. Further reviews were performed on 24 papers that were selected for assessment of the full text. A total of 11 studies met the eligibility criteria. The flow diagram in Figure 1 demonstrates an overview of the study selection process.
Study flow chart

An overview of the included studies is provided in Table 1. All 11 studies were carried out in different hospital settings across India. This table summarizes the design, context, intervention, and results of 11 hospital-based Indian studies. It shows diverse ASP strategies such as audit-feedback, infection control, and training, with results ranging from AMR trends, mortality, prescription behavior, and expenditure. Given the heterogeneity of included studies and the absence of consistent variance data, results are presented descriptively. Outcomes are summarized using raw percentages, frequencies, and before-after comparisons rather than pooled effect measures.

Swamy et al. found a rise in appropriate use from 66.82% to 86.82% and a reduction in average antibiotics used per patient. Cost outcomes

According to the study by Chowdhury SS et al., the antibiotic cost per ICU admission prior to ASP implementation was Rs. 404.05, which reduced to Rs. 375.61 after ASP implementation. Although the cost differences before and after ASP implementation were not statistically significant, a reduction in the average monthly cost was observed.

Sarang B et al. found in their study that the cost of antibiotic prophylaxis per patient was significantly lower in the guideline-oriented group. According to Singh S et al., the mean monthly cost of restricted drugs significantly reduced by 14.4% following ASP implementation compared to the period before ASP implementation.
Barriers and challenges

There are barriers and challenges in the implementation of an antimicrobial stewardship program. According to Verma M et al., the challenges faced during ASP implementation included issues with real-time data capture and extraction of patient information, inadequate training of treating doctors for rational antimicrobial use, limited involvement of nursing staff in infection control practices, and the absence of an in-hospital pharmacy. Additional difficulties involved long wait times for culture and drug susceptibility test reporting, delays between admission and surgery, and congestion in wards.
Discussion
Clinical outcomes and variability

The implementation of ASP is essential for combating the rising concern of AMR. The AMR patterns in the studies by Bansal N et al. and Zacchaeus NGP et al. showed a reduction in the number of treatment-resistant organisms after the implementation of ASP. However, in the study by Bansal et al., the number of colistin-resistant isolates increased to 43 after implementation. Similarly, Chowdhury SS et al. reported a mix of reductions and increases in resistance patterns, while Rupali P et al. found this rise could reflect transitional barriers in implementation, delays in diagnostic support, or temporary disruptions in clinical workflows during stewardship roll-out. Taken together, these findings suggest that while the majority of studies demonstrated reductions in resistance, three studies showed increases or mixed outcomes, indicating that the impact of ASP implementation on resistance is not uniformly consistent across all hospital settings in India.

No significant differences were observed in the mortality rates of other studies. The infection rates before and after ASP implementation in the study by Bansal N et al. reduced from 2.3 to 1.19 in the Central line associated (CLA) blood stream infections (BSI) group and from 2.28 to 1.88 in the Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) group. However, the number of BSI episodes in the study by Priyadarshi et al. increased from 427 to 542 (a 26.9% increase) following implementation. This unexpected increase may be due to enhanced surveillance and detection post-ASP, or systemic factors such as overcrowding, diagnostic lag, and limited infection control resources.
Prescription practices and cost impact

Rationalizing antimicrobial prescription and effective surveillance of antimicrobial use are required in order to control the emergence of multidrug-resistant organisms. A significant change in prescription patterns was observed in the evaluated studies. The appropriate use of drug dose, the choice, route of administration, indication, and duration improved following the implementation of ASP. Swamy A et al. reported significant improvements in prescribing appropriateness following ASP implementation. Samban SS et al. demonstrated marked improvements in compliance with stewardship recommendations.

Overall reductions in cost postimplementation of ASP were observed in all the studies. Although ASP demonstrated significant improvement in appropriate antimicrobial usage, the challenges reported by Verma M et al. occurred during the process of implementation, which included the lack of an electronic record system, inadequate training for treating doctors, lack of involvement of nursing staff, pharmacy within the hospital, and so on, for rational antimicrobial usage.
Comparison with global ASP models

Compared to global standards, the implementation of ASPs in Indian healthcare institutions (HCIs) remains inadequately studied. While many developed countries have well-established ASP teams, robust surveillance systems, and mandatory reporting mechanisms, an Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) 2013 survey of 20 tertiary care Indian hospitals revealed that only 40% had formal ASP documentation and just 30% had active implementation strategies. Key infrastructure, such as access to infectious disease specialists and clinical pharmacists, was lacking. In contrast, global ASP models emphasize interdisciplinary stewardship teams, routine audit-feedback loops, use of electronic medical records for tracking, and clearly defined outcome metrics.
Policy framework and National Efforts (NAP-AMR, ICMR, NCDC)

Although India has initiated policy-level frameworks like the National Action Plan on AMR (2017-2021), translation into hospital-level action is limited. Capacity-building workshops, tailored hospital antibiograms, and customized antibiotic policies are steps in the right direction but remain far from the widespread, systematic ASP integration seen in high-income countries.
Gaps in literature and future directions

Despite policy-level efforts and growing awareness, there remain significant gaps in the literature regarding the comprehensive implementation and evaluation of ASPs in Indian hospitals. Current studies predominantly focus on structural and process indicators, such as the formation of AMS committees, initiation of prescription audits, or development of hospital antibiograms, rather than robust outcome evaluation. There are limited longitudinal data on the impact of stewardship interventions on clinical outcomes like resistance patterns, patient recovery, or hospital stay durations. Furthermore, evidence around de-escalation practices, adherence to formulary restrictions, or antibiotic consumption trends (especially in non-tertiary care and rural hospitals) is very scarce. Most available data stem from point prevalence surveys, pilot programs, or individual institutional reports, making it difficult to generalize or compare findings at the national level. Additionally, research evaluating the effectiveness of educational and behavioral interventions or the utility of WHO's AWaRe classification in guiding Indian prescribing practices is minimal. These gaps highlight the urgent need for multicenter, standardized studies that incorporate both process and outcome indicators. India's National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR) is a robust, multisectoral framework aligned with the WHO's Global Action Plan. It encompasses six strategic priorities, including a dedicated focus on antimicrobial stewardship across human, animal, environmental, and food sectors, underpinned by the One Health approach. A key component, Strategic Priority, centers on optimizing antimicrobial use, highlighting the critical role of ASP. These programs aim to ensure the judicious use of antimicrobials through evidence-based guidelines, prescription auditing, and promoting adherence to the 5 Ds of stewardship: right Diagnosis, Drug, Dose, Duration, and De-escalation. National guidelines by the National Centre for Disease Control (2016) and ICMR (2017) serve as reference frameworks; however, regional adaptation based on local antibiograms remains essential. Although most studies showed reduced resistance, three reported increases. This may reflect incomplete implementation, delays in diagnostics, high baseline MDR rates, limited stewardship resources, and continued reliance on broad-spectrum agents such as colistin. These findings emphasize that the success of ASP relies not just on the presence of protocols but also on the ability to execute them in full and consistently. National guidelines like the ICMR stewardship guidelines and India's National Action Plan on AMR form an invaluable basis, yet hospital-level adaptation is still patchy. Improving diagnostic infrastructure, following stewardship advice, and investing in multidisciplinary teams are critical to bringing about more uniform results and to avoid the escalation of resistance. In summary, while India's NAP-AMR sets the foundation for effective antimicrobial stewardship, translating policy into practice necessitates integrated efforts involving healthcare professionals, policymakers, and the community to ensure sustainable containment of antimicrobial resistance.

In addition, compulsory use of e-prescriptions with centralized linkage can strengthen surveillance by ensuring that every antibiotic prescription is tracked in real time. Integration of WHO's AWaRe classification within such systems would facilitate early identification of inappropriate or excessive use of higher-tier antibiotics, enabling targeted stewardship interventions. Strengthening hospital-level Drug and Therapeutics Committees (DTCs) is also essential. DTCs can provide regular oversight of antimicrobial prescriptions, evaluate frequently used drugs, and correlate usage patterns with local resistance data, thereby enabling timely stewardship actions.
Conclusion

The implementation of ASP in Indian hospitals has shown overall beneficial outcomes, including reductions in resistance, mortality, costs, and inappropriate prescriptions. However, some studies reported increases in resistance, highlighting variability in results across settings. This underscores the need for standardized implementation strategies, continuous monitoring, and stronger institutional support to ensure consistent effectiveness of ASPs. While the majority of studies demonstrated beneficial outcomes of ASP implementation, a few reported increases in resistance, indicating variability in results across settings. Establishing active Drug and Therapeutics Committees (DTCs) within hospitals is critical to ensure continuous prescription audits, monitor resistance trends, and guide formulary restrictions as part of a sustainable stewardship model. Future stewardship strategies in India should incorporate mandatory e-prescription systems linked to centralized databases to enable routine monitoring of antibiotic use, particularly of Watch and Reserve group antibiotics, in alignment with the AWaRe framework.
