After Bacillus inoculation, TS- and TN-groups had larger Bacillus counts than N-group (Fig. 8a). N-group harbored more diverse bacterial species, including E. coli and S. aureus, while Lactobacillus counts increased rapidly after inoculation in TN- and TS-groups, surpassing N-group (Fig. 8b). Subsequently, the number stabilized and eventually exceeded that in the N-group. Besides, only Lactobacillus was detected in the TN- and TS-groups, whereas anaerobic strains were more abundant in the N-group. In terms of pathogenic bacteria, E. coli counts peaked at 18 h in N-group but declined steadily in TN- and TS-groups (Fig. 8c).

To further understand the variance in the bacterial community structure of 883-feed during fermentation, the principal co-ordinates analysis (PCoA) was performed, and PCoA showed distinct OTU profiles among N-, TS-, and TN-group (Fig. 8d). The changes in family level bacterial communities in 883-feed after fermentation are shown in Fig. 8e. The major family in 883-feed of N-group was Moraxellaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, and Lactobacillaceae. The major family in 883-feed of TS-group was Lactobacillaceae and the major family in 883-feed of TN-group was Lactobacillaceae and Bacillus. Heatmap representation of the clustered distant matrix data was used to visualize the microbial composition of different locations of samples by 16S rRNA sequencing. As shown in Fig. 8f, the microbial communities of the N-group were different compared with those of the TS-group and TN-group at the genus level.

To investigate the microbiota composition in different spatial locations, we calculated the relative abundance of different genus shown in a Sankey diagram (Fig. 8g-i). In the figures, the lines of different colors represent different bacterial genus, and the height of the rectangles indicates the relative abundance in the genus. At the genus level, we found that N-group has a more complex flora variation, and the abundance of Acinetobacter remained high after anaerobic fermentation. The pattern of change in flora in the TS- and TN-groups was consistent with the timing of probiotic addition throughout the experiment. The highest abundance of Bacillus was observed after 6 h of the aerobic phase. After subsequent anaerobic fermentation, the abundance of Pediococcus and Weissella in the TS-group stayed high, while the abundance of Bacillus declined. At the end of fermentation, the abundance of Bacillus in the TN-group stayed high, while the abundance of Acinetobacter decreased. At the genus level, N-group was dominated by Moraxellaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, and Lactobacillaceae, TS-group by Lactobacillaceae, and TN-group by Lactobacillaceae and Bacillaceae. Heatmaps and Sankey diagrams confirmed shifts toward probiotic dominance and pathogen reduction in TS- and TN-groups.
Spearman's correlation analysis

We assessed the relationships between pH, nutrient composition, enzymatic activity, BAs, and antioxidant activity with strains using Spearman's correlation analysis. At 12 h, TAN was positively correlated with Bacillus and Laciplantibacillus, and TVBN was negatively correlated with Paenibacillus and Sphingobacterium. PUT correlated positively with Enterococcus and Chryseobacterium but negatively with Laciplantibacillus and Clostridium. T-AOC was positively correlated with Corynebacterium (Fig. 8j). At 24 h, pH was negatively correlated with Enterococcus. ASP was positively correlated with Laciplantibacillus and Pediococcus, and negatively with Acinetobacter. Enzymatic activity was positively correlated with Bacillus and Laciplantibacillus, and negatively with Acinetobacter. TVBN was negatively correlated with Laciplantibacillus and Staphylococcus, and positively with Enterococcus. Bacillus was negatively correlated with spermidine and MDA. T-AOC was negatively correlated with Acinetobacter and positively with Pediococcus (Fig. 8k).
Discussion

In livestock production, the nutritional value of feed directly influences animal growth and production efficiency. Numerous studies have demonstrated that additional processing of feed prior to feeding:through physical, chemical, or biological methods:can effectively enhance its nutritional properties. For instance, thermal treatment can degrade ANFs and improve protein digestibility (Ruiz-Zambrano et al.), while fermentation can break down cellulose structures and increase probiotic content, thereby promoting gut health (Miraalami et al.). Physical processing methods such as micritization and extrusion can also enhance starch gelatinization and energy utilization efficiency (Gonthier et al.; Liermann et al.). Furthermore, co-fermented feeds have been shown to confer substantial digestive, immune, and intestinal benefits, ultimately improving animal growth performance (Liu et al.; Su et al.). In this study, we employed a two-stage fermentation process:an aerobic phase followed by an anaerobic phase to improve the nutritional value of pig feed.

Conventional fermentation typically requires additional heating to 30-37 C, which substantially increases the time and energy costs (Woo et al.). Therefore, this study firstly considered the fermentation characteristics of probiotics under low-temperature conditions. We found that the selected strains maintained metabolic activities at 20 C. Our Bacillus strains exhibited high protease activities (59.74 U), compared to the B. velezensis Z-1(16.92 U) (Lu et al.), and high-yield protease bacteria from Daqu of ZhangGong Laojiu (75-100 U) (Liu et al.); this may be associated with the regulation of multiple metabolic pathways (Yang et al.). Bioactive enzymes play a crucial role in feed fermentation (Yang et al.), and enzyme activity is widely used as a key criterion for selecting functional fermentation strains (Borah et al.; Wongputtisin et al.). Notably, low-temperature incubation did not substantially reduce the bacteriostatic activity of probiotics, possibly due to the production of antimicrobial peptides by Bacillus and the low-pH environment generated by Lactiplantibacillus via organic acid production (Kiousi et al.).

We also examined lysine utilization and preservative tolerance. Lysine is the first limiting amino acid in pig and poultry diets, and its content directly affects biological value (Goethals et al.). The selected strains did not significantly metabolize lysine (residual > 95%), avoiding lysine depletion during fermentation. Researchers (Lau et al. ) have reported near-complete lysine loss during natural fermentation, whereas probiotic-inoculated fermentation reduced this loss to 10%. Thus, screening for strains that do not utilize lysine is essential. Furthermore, most strains displayed strong tolerance to benzoic acid and sodium benzoate, which are effective antimold agents. This indicated that they could remain metabolically active in feed containing preservatives, ensuring process stability (Perez-Diaz et al.; Zhang et al.). The selected strains significantly improved the nutritional profile of soybean meal, wheat, barley, and DDGS. Fermentation increased CP content and reduced EE, likely due to microbial proliferation and associated protease and lipase activity. Antigenic proteins in SBM and alcohol-soluble proteins in cereals were effectively degraded, probably through enhanced protease activity and acid-mediated protein modification (Park et al.). Such degradation improves feed digestibility and reduces intestinal allergic responses in young animal (Barratt et al.). These results are consistent with the observed enzymatic activity profiles of the selected strains.

Microbial interactions are critical during fermentation. In the aerobic stage, Bacillus influences the subsequent growth of Lactobacillus and the biochemical composition of the fermentation (Garcia et al.). We confirmed that selected Bacillus strains do not inhibit Lactiplantibacillus growth. The optimal pairing identified B. subtilis 3-16 for the aerobic phase and L. plantarum E5 for the anaerobic phase.
Therefore, we conducted a follow-up study to evaluate the effect of the 3-16 and E5 combination on 883-feed after two-stage fermentation.

Two-stage fermentation with this combination significantly increased CP and ASP levels, while reducing CF. In the aerobic phase, Bacillus effectively degraded the plant cell wall structure by secreting protease and cellulase enzymes in abundance, releasing the encapsulated protein fractions (Chen et al.). The anaerobic phase further hydrolyzed proteins into small peptides and amino acids, increasing ASP (Sun et al.). These findings are consistent with previous studies (Shi et al. ; Yao et al.). Importantly, fermentation loss rates were lower than in the natural fermentation of N-group; this is similar to the previous research (Xu et al.).

SDS-PAGE analysis confirmed the degradation of major antigenic proteins. Such proteins can trigger hypersensitivity reactions, intestinal barrier disruption, villus atrophy, and impaired digestion (Li et al.; Wang et al.). Their removal reduces allergic responses in weaned piglets and calves. Previous studies have shown that B. amyloliquefaciens LX-6 can achieve 57-78% degradation of glycinin and beta-conglycinin (Huang et al.; Milmine et al.) Our results reinforce the superior efficiency of microbial multi-enzyme systems compared to heat or single-enzyme treatments.

Oxidative stability is another important quality parameter. MDA is a marker of lipid peroxidation, while T-AOC reflects antioxidant potential (Song and Shurson). Although MDA levels increased toward the end of fermentation, they remained significantly lower in the two-stage fermentation group than in the control, consistent with other findings (Su et al. ; Wu et al.). Probiotic-associated antioxidant effects may derive from extracellular polysaccharides, vitamins, superoxide dismutase, catalase, and metal-iron chelation (Echegaray et al.; Wang et al.). Protease activity increased by 64.29% (TS-group), and amylase activity increased by 28.3% (TS-group), following two-stage fermentation, that lead to improved feed digestibility (Gao et al.). Four BAs, such as histamine, tyramine, putrescine, are harmful nitrogenous compounds formed via microbial amino acid decarboxylation (Silla Santos). They can reduce feed intake, impair nutrient absorption, and cause toxicity (Ruiz-Capillas and Herrero). In our study, BAs levels remained low, with total volatile basic nitrogen significantly reduced in two-stage fermentation compared to N-group. This likely reflects both competitive inhibition of BAs-producing microbes and pH reduction by lactic acid bacteria (Incili et al.; Li et al.).

passages.text: Microbial community analysis revealed a reduction in E. coli and other conditionally pathogenic bacteria in two-stage fermentation, alongside increased abundances of Lactobacillus, Bacillus, and Weissella. These shifts are consistent with prior reports (Li et al.). The antimicrobial activity of Bacillus (Caulier et al.) and lactic acid bacteria likely contributed to pathogen suppression (Caulier et al.). Spearman's correlation analysis further indicated that Laciplantibacillus abundance positively correlated with TAN, ASP, and enzyme activity, but negatively with TVBN, PUT, and SPE, consistent with previous studies (Dong et al.; Luo et al.; Zhao et al.). Bacillus abundance positively correlated with TAN and amylase activity and negatively with MDA, aligning with findings by previous study (Peng et al. ). Conversely, Acinetobacter dominant in the N-group showed positive correlations with BAs levels and negative correlations with nutritional and enzymatic indices. Effective fermentation markedly suppressed Acinetobacter growth (Visca et al.). These experimental data suggest that fermentation without probiotic supplementation results in the production of significant quantities of pathogenic bacteria and BAs, which accelerates feed spoilage. In contrast, fermentation supplemented with effective probiotics ensures successful fermentation.

Overall, two-stage fermentation with B. subtilis 3-16 and L. plantarum E5 effectively enhanced nutrient composition, enzymatic activity, antioxidant potential, and microbial quality of pig feed while reducing ANFs and harmful microbial metabolites.
Conclusion

In conclusion, B. subtilis 3-16 exhibits great biological enzyme activity and effectively degrades antigenic factors. L. plantarum E5 produces strong acids and can effectively inhibit the growth of pathogenic bacteria. Our results showed that using a two-stage fermentation mode with 3-16 and E5 (first aerobic, then anaerobic) could significantly improve the nutrient content of complete pig feed. After fermentation, the CP, ASP, and TAN of the pig feed were significantly enhanced, and the antigenic proteins were almost completely degraded. Antioxidant and enzyme activities improved after fermentation. The number of pathogenic bacteria decreased significantly, while the number of beneficial bacteria increased significantly during fermentation. This study provides a foundation for the practical production and application of two-stage co-fermented liquid feed.

passages.text: Intramuscular delivery of mRNA-encoded single-chain variable fragments prevents myotoxin II-induced skeletal muscle damage in a preclinical model

Antivenom is the only effective treatment for snakebites, but it often fails to tackle venom-induced local tissue/muscle damage, leading to permanent disabilities. We investigated whether monoclonal single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) targeting myotoxin II (M-II) from Bothrops asper venom, delivered via mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), could neutralise M-II-induced adverse effects under diverse settings. Human cultured myotubes transfected with mRNA-LNPs expressed scFvs within 24 h and showed resistance to both M-II and venom. In a mouse model, a single intramuscular injection of mRNA-LNPs prompted scFv expression within 48 h and protected against M-II-induced damage. This approach reduced biomarkers for muscle injury, myonecrosis, and damage to the basement membrane and vasculature. This study demonstrates the use of mRNA technology in snakebite management, serving as a proof of concept to improve treatments for envenomings. Although a prophylactic approach may not be feasible for snakebites, prompt delivery of antibodies at the bite site might improve patient outcomes.

Snakebites cause over 140 000 deaths and 400 000 disabilities globally each year. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent the severe effects of envenomings. In this study, we examined the potential benefits of using mRNA technology to express toxin-specific antibody fragments in local tissues and showed their effectiveness in reducing venom-induced muscle damage.
Introduction

Snakebites represent a significant, yet often overlooked global health crisis, which disproportionately impacts impoverished rural communities. Annually, an estimated 5.4 million individuals sustain snakebites, resulting in around 140 000 deaths and 40 0000 permanent disabilities. Although life saving, conventional antivenom treatment is fraught with limitations, including high production costs, limited efficacy against diverse venoms (see Glossary), a risk of causing severe adverse reactions, and low efficacy in managing local manifestations around the bite site. Indeed, antivenoms have proven to be ineffective in preventing snakebite-induced local muscle damage, necessitating the use of various surgical procedures to address this issue. These challenges emphasise the urgent need for the development of more effective, safer, and accessible therapeutic interventions for snakebites, specifically for local envenoming effects. In recent years, there has been an increased focus on the use of advanced biotechnological approaches to counteract the effects of snakebites. One promising avenue is the use of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and single-domain antibodies, which offer high specificity and potency against venom toxins and can be manufactured with limited batch-to-batch variations anda high therapeutic content. However, the manufacturing of mAbs takes many weeks, and they must be physically available at clinics in rural settings where envenomed patients need them promptly.

To explore a unique alternative to conventional antivenom, we investigated the use of mRNA technology combined with lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to express and deliver venom-neutralising antibodies (in scFv format) in local tissues where many snake venom toxins are stored and exert their deleterious effects. The use of mRNA technology for snakebites has not previously been explored and, thus, this study serves as proof of principle for the delivery of antibody-encoding genetic material as a potential treatment. This method leverages the ability of mRNA to be translated into functional proteins within host cells, enabling the in situ and timely expression of therapeutic antibodies. Encapsulating the mRNA in LNPs protects it from degradation and facilitates cellular uptake. This system not only ensures efficient intracellular antibody expression, but has also been proven to be scalable and cost-effective to manufacture. The versatility of mRNA-LNP technology even allows for point-of-demand pharmaceutical production in multipurpose facilities that are widely available in many countries. Our approach builds on recent advances in mRNA vaccine technology, which were extensively validated during the Coronavirus 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. By repurposing this technology, we explored whether mRNA-encoded mAbs (in the form of scFvs) can neutralise snake venom toxins in both in vitro and in vivo settings. For this purpose, we used a myotoxin, M-II [a noncatalytic phospholipase A2-like (PLA2-like) toxin] from the venom of the lancehead viper, Bothrops asper, which is known to cause extensive skeletal muscle damage, harmful effects that the currently used antivenom is unable to mitigate fully. Our study demonstrates the expression of M-II-specific mRNA-encoded scFvs in cultured human myoblasts and the tibialis anterior (TA) muscle in mice, as well as their ability to protect successfully against M-II-induced skeletal muscle damage. These findings highlight the potential utility of mRNA-based therapeutics for preventing venom-induced local tissue damage, although further assessment is needed to determine their applicability in real-life settings.
Results
Encapsulation of mRNA using LNPs

mRNA-loaded LNPs were synthesised with a clinically approved lipid composition using established methods, based on the Moderna SpikeVax COVID-19 vaccine (Table S1 in the supplemental information online). mRNA-LNPs showed sizes, size polydispersities, and zeta potentials similar to those previously reported. We encapsulated two distinct mRNA constructs: one encoding scFvs targeting M-II, and the other encoding scFvs directed against alpha-cobratoxin (alpha-ctx), which served as an unrelated control in this study. Both mRNAs exhibited an encapsulation efficiency (EE%) of ~98% (Table S2 in the supplemental information online). Overall, these data suggest that the mRNA-LNPs synthesised were of high quality and suitable for further analysis.
mRNA-LNPs induce scFv expression in cultured human myotubes

To determine whether mRNA-LNPs can induce the expression of scFvs in cultured cells, transfection was performed in human AB1190 myotubes (originally developed using isolated cells from the paraventral muscle of a 16-year-old male and maintained for research purposes). The culture medium from myotubes was collected 24 h after the cells were transfected with mRNA-LNPs (1 mug/ml). The successful expression of M-II-specific scFvs was confirmed by a selective immunoassay (Figure 1A). Detectable levels of scFvs were also observed in the supernatant of cells incubated with mRNA encoding the alpha-ctx-specific scFvs as unrelated controls (Figure S1 in the supplemental information online). The nontransfected myotubes used as a control did not express any such scFvs. In addition, the transfection of mRNA-LNPs (1 mug/ml) into fully differentiated myotubes did not alter their morphology or size (Figure 1B). These data demonstrate that transfection of mRNA-LNPs does not affect the properties of cultured myotubes and that mRNA-LNPs induce the expression of scFvs at detectable levels under in vitro conditions.
scFvs produced in myotubes prevent damage induced by M-II and B. asper venom

Following confirmation of the expression of scFvs, we examined their neutralising potential against M-II in cultured myotubes. Both control and mRNA-LNPs targeting M-II (1 mug/ml)-transfected myotubes exhibited similar myosin heavy chain (MyHC)-positive areas characterised by long, cylindrical, and multinucleated structures (Figure 1C). Here, no obvious toxic effects were observed in the transfected myotubes. Treatment with B. asper venom (1.25 mug/ml) and M-II (1.25 mug/ml) significantly reduced the size and coverage of the myotubes (Figure 1C,D). The concentrations of venom and M-II for this study were selected based on a titration experiment in cultured myotubes (Figure S2 in the supplemental information online). Venom induced more damage to myotubes compared with M-II. As expected, the impact of venom and M-II on mRNA-LNP-transfected myotubes was significantly reduced due to the presence of scFvs targeting M-II. The mean coverage of MyHC in myotubes incubated with B. asper venom and M-II was 9.56% and 14.53%, respectively. However, myotubes preincubated with mRNA-LNPs exhibited a mean coverage of 22.16% and 31.71% after 24 h of exposure to venom and M-II, respectively. These data demonstrate that the scFvs produced through transfected mRNA-LNPs offer protective effects against venom- and M-II-induced damage in cultured myotubes. Notably, relatively less neutralising effects (evidenced by smaller myotube coverage) were observed for venom than for M-II. This is likely because the venom is a complex mixture of toxins that can exert synergistic effects by damaging myotubes and disrupting the interactions between mature myotubes and the plate surface, leading to detachment and cell death.

Notably, myotubes transfected with unrelated mRNA exhibited markedly reduced coverage following treatment with M-II, indicating that protection depends on the specificity of the encoded scFvs (Figure S3A in the supplemental information online). Likewise, LNPs without mRNA did not provide any protective effect (Figure S3B). Consistent with these findings, B. asper venom and M-II elicited a pronounced release of muscle damage-related biomarkers (Figure 1E,F) into the myotube culture supernatant, which was markedly attenuated by expressed scFvs targeting M-II following transfection. By contrast, unrelated mRNA or empty LNPs failed to preserve muscle cell viability and membrane integrity in the presence of M-II (Figure S4 in the supplemental information online), indicating that they do not exert any effects against M-II-induced muscle damage.
Concentrations of mRNA-LNPs have a critical role in controlling scFv levels

The actions of mRNA-LNPs are usually concentration dependent, requiring a delicate balance between their activity and toxicity. Therefore, we assessed whether different amounts of mRNA-LNPs can increase the expression of scFvs and improve their neutralising potential. The transfection of myotubes with three different concentrations (1, 2.5, and 5 mug/ml) of mRNA-LNPs resulted in varying levels of scFvs (Figure 2A; Figure S1 for the unspecific mRNA-LNPs). While 2.5 mug/ml of mRNA-LNPs displayed the highest level of scFvs, 5 mug/ml of mRNA-LNPs displayed a nonsignificant level of scFvs compared with the negative control. In line with these data, M-II-specific mRNA-LNPs at 1 and 2.5 mug/ml provided significant protection against M-II-induced damage on myotubes, although 5 mug/ml displayed toxicity with noticeable changes to the myotube architecture (Figure 2B). Microscopic images (Figure 2B) as well as the quantification of MyHC-positive area suggested that using 5 mug/ml of mRNA-LNPs induced toxicity and affected the viability of myotubes (Figure 2C). Pre-incubation of mature myotubes with 5 mug/ml mRNA-LNPs reduced the MyHC-positive area to 42%. Further addition of M-II to these myotubesled to a greater reduction in myotube area (MyHC-positive area of 6.29%). These data suggest that optimisation of the concentrations of mRNA-LNPs is essential to ensure optimum levels of scFvs and minimise the toxicity of LNP-based delivery systems. High concentrations of mRNA-LNPs are likely to induce cytotoxic effects on myotubes, which will ultimately affect the expression of scFvs. Further analysis of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (Figure 2D) and creatine kinase (CK) (Figure 2E) in the culture medium revealed markedly elevated levels of these enzymes at the high (5 mug/ml) concentration of mRNA-LNPs. Similar increases in LDH were observed when equivalent amounts of unrelated mRNA or empty LNPs were transfected into myotubes (Figure S4). Together, these data indicate that fully differentiated human myotubes are sensitive to high amounts of LNP formulation, which results in cytotoxicity.

passages.text: mRNA-LNPs require at least 12 h to express sufficient levels of scFvs to exert protective effects

Following transfection, the scFvs need to be expressed and released into the surrounding medium. This process may take several hours, depending on various factors, including the size of the mRNA construct. To gain insights into the kinetics of M-II-specific scFv expression, we evaluated different incubation periods before treatment with M-II. The addition of M-II at 0, 3, and 6 h following transfection with mRNA-LNPs (1 mug/ml) significantly affected the myotubes, similar to the controls without mRNA-LNPs (Figure 3A). However, the protective effects of scFvs were evident at 12 and 24 h following transfection with mRNA-LNPs in myotubes. When the myotubes were treated with venom, the protective effects were observed only at 24 h (Figure 3B). These data demonstrate that the mRNA-LNPs require at least 12-24 h to express sufficient levels of scFvs that can offer protective effects against M-II or the venom under in vitro settings. This protective effect was corroborated by quantifying the release of LDH and CK into the culture medium (Figure 3C-F). Significantly reduced levels of these enzymes were observed at 12 and 24 h post transfection with mRNA-LNPs.
Intramuscular administration of mRNA-LNPs protects against M-II-induced muscle damage in mice

Based on the above data, we analysed the protective effects of mRNA-LNPs (3.4 mug/mouse) in a venom-induced muscle damage model in mice using M-II. The mice were divided into different groups: mRNA-LNPs alone [one encoding scFvs targeting M-II and another for a neurotoxin (alpha-ctx)]; M-II alone; and mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II. The mRNA-LNPs were injected intramuscularly (i.m.) into the TA muscle of mice on Day 0. Then, M-II (50 mug/20 g mouse) was administered i.m. on Day 2 (i.e., after 48 h to allow sufficient expression of scFvs) (Figure 4A). The TA muscles from mice were collected on Day 3 (i.e., 24 h after treatment with M-II). As expected, mice treated with M-II did not express any scFvs in circulating plasma, whereas injection of mRNA-LNPs in control mice displayed a high level of circulating scFvs (Figure 4B). The mice treated mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II showed slightly reduced plasma levels of unbound scFvs, which could be due to their binding to M-II, although this requires further investigation. In agreement with this speculation, elevated levels of scFvs were observed in the group treated with mRNA-LNPs encoding scFvs against alpha-ctx (Figure S5 in the supplemental information online). Moreover, quantification of biomarkers, such as CK (Figure 4C) and LDH (Figure 4D), confirmed the protective effects of scFvs in mice treated with mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II. Indeed, M-II injection led to a significant increase in these biomarkers, which are reduced by the scFvs. The TA muscles treated only with M-II were slightly heavier than those from controls and from mice treated with mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II (Figure 4E). These data demonstrate that tissue swelling that may result from the influx of immune cells and fluids at the injured area, as well as elevated biomarkers for muscle damage following M-II injection, alongside the protective effects of scFvs. Mice injected with unrelated mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II-induced injury displayed muscle weight changes comparable to those receiving M-II alone, indicating that protection depends on the specificity of the expressed scFvs (Figure S6 in the supplemental information online).

Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining of TA muscle sections in M-II-treated mice demonstrated a significant area of myonecrosis, interstitial space, and infiltration of immune cells compared with controls (Figure 4F). However, the level of damage was reduced in the group to which M-II-specific mRNA-LNPs were administered to express scFvs. All groups exhibited a comparable fibre size distribution (Figure S7 in the supplemental information online). Although not statistically significant, the M-II group showed a slight reduction in fibre count, suggesting that some fibres were already damaged or undergoing lysis, but had not yet been cleared or fully degraded, which is consistent with histological findings from sections collected 1 day post injection of M-II (Figure 4F). A high level of IgG-infiltrated fibres (indicative of damaged fibres) was observed in M-II-treated mice, but the mRNA-LNPs targeting M-II largely reduced this effect (Figure 4G). Similarly, the expression of dystrophin remained intact in the control muscle but was decreased by M-II. However, the administration of mRNA-LNPs resulted in an expanded distribution of structurally intact dystrophin (Figure 4H). Both groups of mice treated with mRNA-LNPs displayed signs of infiltrating immune cells with a small area of damage (Figure S8 in the supplemental information online). No neutralisation of M-II toxicity was observed in mice pretreated with mRNA-LNPs for alpha-ctx (Figure S9 in the supplemental information online). H&E staining and quantification of IgG-infiltrated fibres and dystrophin-positive areas in mice treated with alpha-ctx-specific mRNA-LNPs, followed by M-II, revealed muscle damage comparable with that of M-II alone. In line with in vitro findings from cultured myotubes, these data emphasise the successful delivery of M-II-specific mRNA-LNPs and the subsequent expression of scFvs to protect against M-II-induced muscle damage in mice. The unrelated mRNA-LNPs and resulting scFvs did not exert any protective effects against M-II-induced muscle damage.

passages.text: scFvs prevent the degradation of extracellular matrix components

The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a critical factor in promoting successful muscle regeneration following acute damage. Hence, we evaluated the impact of M-II on ECM components (laminin and collagen IV) and the ability of the scFv-encoding mRNA-LNPs to protect them. M-II-treated mice displayed variable fibre sizes and diameters as well as a slight (nonsignificant) reduction in laminin levels (Figure 5A). Necrotic areas of these muscle sections displayed interruptions in the immunostaining of laminin around some fibres. By contrast, the control (mRNA-LNPs) mice and those treated with mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II exhibited a more uniform pattern and intensity of laminin staining, with fewer areas showing spatially heterogeneous laminin expression. The expression of laminin was uniform in the control group. However, a discontinuous expression of laminin was observed in M-II-treated mice, which was restored by scFv-encoding mRNA-LNPs (Figure 5B). Similarly, a low (nonsignificant) level of collagen IV was observed in M-II-treated muscle sections, but this was improved by scFv-encoding mRNA-LNPs (Figure 5C). Similar to laminin, the expression of collagen IV was uniform in the control and mRNA-LNP-treated muscle, but was not uniform in M-II-treated muscle, with reduced grey values (Figure 5D). Overall, the muscle sections from mRNA-LNP pretreated groups exhibited large areas with uniform and higher intensity staining, consistent with the trend observed for laminin (Figure 5B).

In summary, the analysis of basement membrane components revealed a slight decrease in collagen IV and laminin content within necrotic muscle fibre areas in M-II-treated mice. However, the mRNA-LNP-treated groups exhibited a highly preserved and structurally intact extracellular ECM scaffold, characterised by a uniform distribution of collagen IV and laminin without interruptions in expression patterns, and homogeneous thickness and intensity. These data were corroborated by picrosirius red staining in muscle sections, where the architecture of collagen in mRNA-LNP-treated mice before M-II administration appeared to be similar to that in mRNA-LNP-alone controls (Figure 5E).
scFvs reduce intramuscular bleeding and blood vessel damage

The clearance of intramuscular bleeding or thrombi and angiogenesis is critical to promote muscle regeneration. Thus, we examined the intramuscular presence of fibrinogen (as a marker of bleeding and thrombi) and CD31 (a marker of angiogenesis) in TA muscle sections. Administration of M-II resulted in an increased area of fibrinogen staining in muscle sections (Figure 6A,B). However, this was largely reduced by the scFv-encoding mRNA-LNPs. Similarly, the M-II-treated muscle sections exhibited an irregular distribution and decreased expression of CD31, although this was improved by the scFv-encoding mRNA-LNPs (Figure 6C,D). These findings align with the disruption of standard muscle architecture and the presence of an extensive necrotic environment in M-II-treated muscle, as reported above. Overall, these data demonstrate the impact of mRNA-LNP-delivered scFvs in protecting skeletal muscle against the M-II-induced damage.
Discussion

Since snakebites predominantly affect rural communities, which often have limited access to medical infrastructure, prompt treatment following bites is critical to prevent venom-induced complications and subsequent deaths, disabilities, and long-term health consequences. Conventional plasma-derived immunoglobulins (antivenoms) are effective in neutralising freely available venom toxins found in the circulation. Therefore, they act as the primary treatment for systemic effects caused by snakebites. However, antivenoms fail to tackle snakebite-induced local muscle damage mainly due to the interruption of blood supply and the prolonged action of tissue-bound venom toxins, causing continuous cycles of muscle degeneration and regeneration. Notably, the fast-acting nature of venom toxins makes it challenging to prevent local tissue damage caused by snakebites. For example, the venom of B. asper contains several toxins that rapidly damage tissues, resulting in complex pathological changes that hinder the innate regeneration of skeletal muscle. Myotoxic PLA2s and PLA2-like proteins in snake venoms have a key role in this pathological process and, therefore, are important toxin targets for effective snakebite treatment. In this study, we used a robust preclinical model to investigate the potential of using mRNA-LNP-delivered scFvs as a new avenue to develop target-specific antibody therapy to prevent venom-induced muscle damage.

The intramuscular administration of mRNAs as vaccines in humans has been used for some time to offer passive immunisation against invading pathogens. Indeed, this approach has been widely used to protect against COVID-19. Here, we investigated the potential of an mRNA construct designed to express M-II-specific scFvs to protect against M-II-induced muscle damage. The delivery of mRNA-LNPs and the expression of scFvs were initially achieved using cultured human myotubes. The mRNA-LNP formulation successfully entered the myotubes and generated scFvs, with detectable levels in the media. These data are similar to previously reported findings that demonstrate the feasibility of using mRNA constructs to express target proteins in host systems. The expressed scFvs displayed notable protection against M-II-induced damage in cultured myotubes, when these were challenged with either toxin alone or with whole venom. The concentrations and time points required for mRNA to express sufficient levels of scFvs were analysed. Our data demonstrate that higher concentrations of mRNA-LNPs induced toxic effects in myotubes, while low concentrations generated significant levels of scFvs without any cytotoxic effects. Other studies using mRNA-LNPs to tackle infectious diseases have also observed such concentration-dependent toxicity in different cell types. Moreover, administration of our mRNA-LNP-delivered scFvs led to protective outcomes only after 12-24 h of administration. This situation could present a challenge when managing snake-bite complications that require emergency actions. However, in the absence of other therapeutic options, the administration of mRNA-encoded antibodies could still provide protection, given that snake venom toxins are known to remain in muscle tissues and exert their function for prolonged periods.

passages.text: mRNA-LNP treatment protected myotubes from both M-II alone and B. asper venom-induced damage. However, complete neutralisation was not observed, and the protective effects were less pronounced when mRNA-transfected myotubes were exposed to the whole venom, which contains multiple types of toxin from different protein families, of which several affect plasma membrane and basement membrane components. This points to the future challenge of mitigating a wider range of toxic effects caused by multiple components in snake venoms. Moreover, different toxins can act alone or in synergy in host tissues, leading to a diverse spectrum of clinical manifestations. The presence of multiple isoforms of toxins without well-defined structure-activity relationships, combined with several toxin families, creates additional challenges for the clinical use of single-target strategies as the primary treatment for snakebites. However, mRNA technology is a novel avenue to explore for delivering therapeutic levels of antibodies under a broad range of conditions. It can likely be optimised by using mRNAs encoding oligoclonal broadly neutralising antibodies against multiple toxins, analogous to what has been demonstrated using oligoclonal human immunoglobulin G antibodies and camelid single-domain antibodies. Specifically, the latter approach has been successful in reducing the tissue damage caused by myotoxic PLA2s from Bothrops venoms.

The mRNA-LNPs alone elicited a minor inflammatory response at the injection site in the TA muscle of mice. Previous studies using this platform for other indications have also reported similar local reactions at the injection site of the mRNA-LNPs. M-II induces typical muscle toxicity caused by snake venom PLA2s with increased levels of CK and LDH, myonecrosis, and low dystrophin expression. The reduction of necrotic areas and IgG-infiltrated fibres in H&E muscle sections and the high-level expression of dystrophin in mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II-treated mice corroborate the in vitro neutralisation ability of scFvs against M-II on cultured myotubes. In addition, we identified that M-II led to a necrotic environment characterised by lower expression of basement membrane components, such as collagen-IV and laminin. Although M-II does not have proteolytic activity, previous studies reported its impact on the ECM, which was attributed to the modulation and activation of matrix metalloproteases that are involved in tissue remodelling in necrotic areas of injured muscles. An irregular expression of CD31 and elevated fibrinogen levels were observed in the M-II-treated muscle. However, the mRNA-LNP-delivered scFvs prevented these changes in ECM proteins, angiogenesis, and bleeding, which was consistent with the less extensive muscle damage. Hence, this approach may help enable the local expression of neutralising scFvs in damaged muscles, which intravenously administered immunoglobulins or their Fab fragments often fail to reach.

Several limitations are associated with this study, which warrant further investigation. The mRNA-encoded scFvs had to be made available in advance in tissues to neutralise venom toxins in the models used here. This may not be superior to, or even on par with, traditional antivenoms, which immediately neutralise toxins upon intravenous administration. We hypothesise that, in potential scenarios where antivenom is unavailable but mRNA-LNPs can be synthesised and administered on-site, this approach might find utility. The combined use of antivenom and mRNA-LNPs could also be used to tackle both systemic and local envenoming effects, compensating for the low tissue penetration of some antibodies with in situ expression and the time delay in expressing these scFvs. mRNA-LNPs can ensure the active expression of antibodies over a longer period, complementing the rapid decay of passively administered antibodies or fragments thereof present in traditional antivenoms and/or recombinant antivenoms. Moreover, mRNAs encoding antibodies targeting multiple toxins in venoms are likely needed to ensure sufficient neutralisation of all medically relevant toxins. Finally, the storage of mRNA-LNPs in rural settings with a limited infrastructure is a major concern. However, this can be addressed with the support of government health authorities in terms of practical implementation.

Our findings demonstrate that mRNA-LNP technology can be used to generate scFvs in situ and that these scFvs can prevent M-II-induced muscle damage under in vitro and in vivo settings when delivered in advance of the toxin challenge. This warrants further research to establish whether antibody-encoding mRNAs delivered via LNPs could find utility as an alternative to, or in combination with, antibody-based therapy against snakebites, particularly for local envenoming effects, such as muscle damage, which are not effectively tackled by conventional antivenoms.
Concluding remarks
Although mRNA technology advanced rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, its use in addressing complex conditions, such as snakebites, remains largely unexplored. The findings

presented here provide preliminary support for a potential new therapeutic approach, in which toxin-specific antibodies are expressed locally within tissues near the bite site. This strategy may enhance the neutralisation of locally acting toxins. Unlike conventional animal-derived antivenoms, which often exhibit limited efficacy at the bite site, localised antibody expression could complement existing treatments by promoting more effective toxin neutralisation where it is most needed. Further studies will be necessary to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and therapeutic potential of this approach in appropriate preclinical models (see Outstanding questions).

Method Details
Design of mRNA constructs

Two mRNA constructs were designed with a myostatin leader sequence (MQKLQLCVYIYLFMLIVAGPVDL) in front of the anti-M-II or anti-alpha-ctx scFv genes, followed by a 3xFLAG tag (DYKDHDGDYKDHDIDYKDDDDK). Synthetic mRNAs were ordered from TebuBio with the following modifications: Full Substitution of N1-Methyl-Pseudo-U, Capped (Cap 1) using CleanCap  AG (3'OMe), Polyadenylated (120A), DNase and Phosphatase Treatment, and Silica Membrane Purification.
Encapsulation of synthetic mRNAs into LNPs
Formulation of lipid nanoparticles

mRNA molecules were dissolved in an aqueous phase of 25 mM sodium acetate buffer (SAB), pH 5. Lipids were dissolved in an organic phase of absolute ethanol. The LNPs were made of lipids SM-102 (heptadecan-9-yl 8-(2-hydroxyethyl) [6-oxo-6-(undecyloxy)hexyl]aminooctanoate), DSPC (1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine), cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000 (1,2-dimyristoyl-rac-glycero-3-methoxypolyethylene glycol-2000) in a ratio of 50:10:38.5:1.5. The formulations were prepared using the NanoAssemblr Platform (Precision Nanosystems Inc., Vancouver, Canada) with a staggered herringbone micromixer. The aqueous phase and organic phase were injected in a ratio of 3:1 at a flow rate of 12 ml/min with an N:P ratio of 6:1. Particles were collected in a 15 ml Falcon tube, transferred to a 10,000 MW cutoff dialysis chamber, and dialysed again in 20 mM Tris for 16 hours at 4 C.
DLS and zeta potential

Particles were diluted 100 times in 20 mM Tris to a volume of 1 ml in a 1 cm cuvette and measured using the Zetasizer Nano ZS (Malvern Panalytical, Egham, Surrey). The mRNA-LNPs had physical properties (size, polydispersity index, surface charge, and encapsulation efficiency) similar to those previously reported by other groups, being approximately 70-90 nm in diameter, with a PDI below 0.2, a surface charge between 0 and - 3 mV, and an encapsulation efficiency above 90%.
Encapsulation efficiency

The mRNA encapsulation efficiency was examined by using the RiboGreen assay according to the manufacturer's instructions. The samples were diluted to a concentration of approximately 50 ng/ml in a TE buffer solution. 50 muL of the diluted samples were transferred to a polystyrene 96-well plate (Corning, Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), and either 50 muL of TE buffer or 50 muL of a 1% (v/v) Triton X-100, Hydrogenated, PROTEIN GRADE , solution (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany) was added to the wells. The plate was incubated at 37 C for 15 minutes. The RiboGreen reagent was diluted 1:1000 in 1X Tris EDTA (TE) buffer, and 100 muL of this solution was added to each well. The fluorescence intensity was measured using a fluorescence plate reader (Spark  multimode microplate reader, Tecan Trading AG, Switzerland) at an excitation wavelength of 500 nm and an emission wavelength of 530 nm. The fluorescence values of the reagent blank were subtracted from those of each of the samples, and the percentage of free RNA was determined by dividing the fluorescence intensity of the intact sample (without the addition of Triton X-100) by the fluorescence value of the disrupted sample (caused by the addition of Triton X-100) using standard curves.
Cell culture and transfection of mRNA-LNPs

The AB1190 human myoblasts were routinely maintained in 75 cm2 cell culture flasks and cultured in a growth medium with the supplement mix (PromoCell, Germany). To obtain myotubes for transfection, 50,000 cells were incubated for two days in growth media. Then they (when they reached ~85% confluency) were kept in a differentiation (DMEM) media with 5% (v/v) horse serum for another two days. Posteriorly, the media was replaced with fresh media containing different concentrations of mRNA-LNPs. Empty LNPs were also used as a control. The cultured myotubes were treated with purified M-II or whole venom for various periods. Antibiotics were not used in cell culture to avoid their toxicity and effects on the transfection efficiency of mRNA-LNPs.

passages.text: Immunoassay to quantify scFvs

Following transfection of mRNA-LNPs in myotubes, the clear media was collected at 24 hours along with untransfected negative controls. These media were used to quantify the presence of scFvs by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). A high-binding 96-well plate was coated with diluted media overnight at 4 C before blocking with 5% (w/v) bovine serum albumin for one hour. The plate was then washed three times with 0.1% (v/v) Tween-20 diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Then, 100 mul of diluted primary antibody (rabbit anti-FLAG antibody, Cat. No. F7425-2MG, Sigma-Aldrich, UK) in blocking buffer [5% (w/v) bovine serum albumin (BSA)] was added to each well and incubated for four hours at room temperature. Following three washes with 0.1% (v/v) Tween-20 in PBS, horse-radish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies (goat anti-rabbit IgG H+L, Cat. No. 65-6120, ThermoFisher Scientific, UK) diluted in blocking buffer were added and incubated at room temperature for one hour. The plate was washed three times with 0.1% (v/v) Tween-20 diluted in PBS, and tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) was added as a substrate for HRP. The reaction was stopped with an acidic solution (0.2 M H2SO4), and the absorbance was measured at 450 nm. The controls, including media from non-transfected cells, and only primary or secondary antibodies, were included as specified in our experimental design. The same procedure was used to quantify the scFvs in serum samples from mice.
Assessing the neutralising properties of scFvs

Myoblasts were cultured by seeding 50,000 cells per well and incubating them for two days in a growth medium. After reaching ~85% confluency, the growth medium was replaced with a differentiation medium [high glucose DMEM (Gibco, UK) supplemented with 1% (v/v) penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco, UK) and 5% (v/v) horse serum (Gibco, UK)], to stimulate myotube formation. After 72 hours, fully differentiated myotubes were observed using a bright-field microscope. The media was then refreshed, and mRNA-LNPs were added and incubated for 24 hours. The same volume of LNPs was incubated with myotubes to reproduce the experimental conditions of the mRNA-LNP-treated groups. The mature myotubes were exposed to B. asper venom (1.25 mug/ml) or purified M-II (1.25 mug/ml) for 24 hours, while non-transfected cells served as a control and were evaluated under the same conditions. Venom and toxin concentrations were chosen based on our prior experience with viper venoms in this cell-based screening and an initial concentration-response assessment. The myotubes were fixed using 2% (w/v) paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS, and then immunostaining with pan-myosin (MyHC) antibodies was performed, followed by imaging with a fluorescence microscope (Zeiss AxioImager, UK). The myotube area coverage was analysed using ImageJ. The same protocol was used with different concentrations (1, 2.5, and 5 mug/ml) of mRNA-LNPs and incubation times before adding venom or M-II. The impact of mRNA-LNPs on myotube integrity and viability was assessed by quantifying creatine kinase (CK) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activities using absorbance-based colourimetric assays.
TA muscle damage in mice

All experiments involving mice were performed in line with the principles and guidelines of the British Home Office (PPL70/7516) and the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986. Male C57BL/6 mice (10 weeks old) were sourced from Envigo, UK. The animals were divided into five groups: mRNA-LNPs alone (one group for each mRNA-encoding scFc targeting M-II or alpha-ctx), M-II alone, and mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II. Following anaesthesia with 3.5% isoflurane in oxygen, respective groups received intramuscular injections of 30 muL mRNA-LNPs (3.4 mug/20 g mouse) into their right TA muscle. Two days later, mice from the mRNA-LNPs followed by M-II and M-II alone groups were given intramuscular injections of 30 muL of M-II (50 mug/20 g mouse). After 24 hours of M-II injections, all mice were sacrificed using carbon dioxide and subsequent cervical dislocation. TA muscles were dissected, weighed, and frozen in liquid nitrogen-cooled isopentane and stored in a -80 C freezer. Blood was collected from all mice to measure biomarkers and estimate the levels of scFvs.
Quantification of creatinine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase in mouse serum

The colourimetric measurements of creatinine kinase (CK) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) were performed at the Mary Lyon Centre Clinical Pathology Laboratory (MRC Harwell Institute, UK) on a Beckman Coulter DXC 700 AU Clinical Chemistry Analyser (Beckman Coulter, High Wycombe, UK) using serum samples obtained from mice.
Histological staining and immunohistochemistry of muscle sections

Transverse sections (15 mum thickness) were obtained using a cryo microtome from Tissue-TEK  OCT-mounted muscle tissues and stored at -80 C. Before immunostaining, sections were initially washed with PBS to remove OCT. To visualise the muscle architecture and level of necrosis as well as the collagen organisation, the sections were stained with H&E and picrosirius red, respectively. The extent of injury was calculated as a percentage, taking into account areas including fibrosis, infiltration with immune cells, and necrotic fibres, as described previously. Profiles of the spatial distribution of muscle biomarkers of fibre integrity (dystrophin), necrosis (IgG), integrity of basement membrane components (collagen-IV and laminin), angiogenesis (CD31), and intramuscular bleeding (fibrinogen) were obtained through immunostaining using appropriate antibodies on muscle sections. For immunostaining, after removal of OCT, the muscle sections were incubated in permeabilisation buffer [20 mM HEPES, 3 mM MgCl2, 50 mM NaCl, 0.05% (w/v) sodium azide, 300 mM sucrose, and 0.5% (v/v) Triton X-100] for 15 minutes at room temperature. After washing with PBS (three times, five minutes each), blocking buffer [PBS with 5% (v/v) fetal bovine serum and 0.05% (v/v) Triton X-100] was applied for 30 minutes. Primary antibodies were blocked and applied overnight at 4 C. Secondary antibodies were then used, followed by three washes with PBS. All the images were captured using an All-in-One Fluorescence Microscope (BZ-X800, Keyence, Japan).
Quantification And Statistical Analysis
The BZ-X800 Analyser, ImageJ, and Cellpose software were used for processing and analysing the images. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Inc., USA).

Highlights
Snakebites are a major public health concern, impacting millions of lives in rural areas globally.
Obtaining animal-derived antivenom treatment immediately after sustaining a snakebite is challenging due to various practical difficulties in rural areas.

We developed mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to express and deliver single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) of antibodies against a venom myotoxin and tested their efficacy in preventing myotoxin and venom-induced muscle damage in vitro and in vivo.
Delivery of the mRNA-LNPs led to expression of scFvs after a time delay, which protected against myotoxin and venom-induced muscle damage in mice.
Technology readiness

We demonstrated that our mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology is able to express toxin-specific antibodies in tissues to neutralise venom components after a snakebite, achieving a technology readiness level (TRL) of 4. Through in vitro experiments with cultured myoblasts and myotubes, and in vivo studies using suitable animal models, we showed the ability of mRNA-LNPs to mitigate myotoxin- and venom-induced muscle damage. To advance this technology to higher readiness levels, mRNA-encoded antibodies targeting multiple key toxins, along with strategies for their rapid deployment in rural settings following snakebite, should be further developed and evaluated. Key challenges, such as production costs, thermostability, the time required to express sufficient amounts of antibodies, and practical difficulties in administering mRNA-LNPs in humans, must be addressed before field testing this technology.
Glossary
mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (LNPs): mRNA molecules designed to express a protein (in this study, antibody fragments) that are encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles to help them enter cells.
Myotoxin: an isolated toxin from a specific snake venom that can cause muscle damage.

Single-chain variable fragments (scFvs): these are single-chain variable fragments of antibodies capable of binding to specific regions of target antigens or proteins that they have been designed against.
Transfection: a process by which genetic material, such as mRNA, can be introduced into cells.
Venom: a mixture of toxins produced by specialised venom glands in animals, such as snakes and certain invertebrate species; used to capture prey and for defence.
Outstanding questions
What antibody format is the most optimal to use for delivery using mRNA-LNP technology?
How can we design a cocktail of mRNA-LNPs that deliver antibodies against all medically relevant toxins in snake venoms?
How can we address the challenges of venom variability by selecting broadly neutralising antibodies to be delivered by mRNA-LNPs?
How can we decrease the time needed to produce sufficient quantities of antibodies to neutralise the toxins despite the varying amounts of venom injected during snakebites?
How quickly do we need to administer mRNA-LNPs after snakebites before the effects of envenoming worsen?
What are the cost implications and practical challenges of using mRNA-LNPs to treat snakebite patients in rural settings?

passages.text: Asparaginase Hypersensitivity Reactions in NK/T-Cell Lymphomas

Background/Objectives: Asparaginase (ASP)-based chemotherapy has substantially improved clinical outcomes in Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive NK/T-cell lymphomas (NKTCL). However, as a bacterial-derived enzyme, ASP is frequently associated with immune-mediated adverse events, particularly hypersensitivity reactions (HSRs), which may compromise both treatment efficacy and patient safety. This report presents a case of an ASP-related HSR and reviews the incidence within our institutional cohort. Detailed Case Description: A 60-year-old female presented an immediate Grade 2 HSR during her second PEG-asparaginase infusion, with pruritus, vomiting, and presyncope. The infusion was discontinued, and she was subsequently transitioned to crisantaspase:an alternative formulation:which was well tolerated without further adverse events. She remains disease-free to date. A retrospective review of institutional records (2015-2025) identified six patients with NKTCL treated with ASP-containing chemotherapy. The incidence of HSRs in this cohort was 1 of 6 (16.7%). Conclusions: As in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, HSRs to asparaginase remains a major challenge in the management of NKTCL with potential implications for treatment safety and efficacy. The establishment of standardized, consensus-based criteria for the diagnosis, classification, and management of ASP-related HSRs is urgently needed to optimize patient outcomes.
1. Introduction

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive NK/T-cell lymphomas (NKTCL) are highly aggressive neoplasms encompassing both EBV-positive nodal T- and NK-cell lymphoma and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, formerly referred to as the nasal type. These malignancies represent approximately 10% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHL) in Asia and several Latin American countries, but are rare in the United States, accounting for only 1-2% of NKTCL and just 0.2% of all NHL. Their incidence is, however, markedly higher among Hispanic and Asian/Pacific Islander individuals. A recent German study reports an annual incidence of 0.77 per 100,000 people.

Multiple prognostic scores have been described to stratify patient outcomes. Recently, the incorporation of beta-2-microglobulin into the Prognostic Index of Natural Killer Lymphoma (PINK-B) has been shown to improve discrimination, as significant differences in three-year outcomes were observed among risk groups. Overall survival (OS) reached 84.1% in low-risk, 46.8% in intermediate-risk, and 17.6% in high-risk patients, While 3-year progression-free survival (PFS) showed a similar gradient, at 70.6%, 35.9%, and 7.3%, respectively. Initially, overexpression of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) was thought to be the main driver of multidrug resistance in extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTCL). However, the poor efficacy of P-gp-independent agents, such as methotrexate and cytarabine, indicates that additional resistance mechanisms are involved, as reflected by the suboptimal clinical outcomes observed with these drugs.

In 2005, selective sensitivity to L-Asparaginasa of ENKTCL cells was demonstrated. Since the incorporation of asparaginase (ASP) into combination regimens, response rates and long-term outcomes have improved substantially. ASP catalyzes the hydrolysis of asparagine, and its depletion in plasma inhibits protein and nucleotide synthesis, ultimately inducing apoptotic death of tumor cells.

Despite its clinical benefit, ASP administration is limited by immune-mediated toxicity. As a bacterial enzyme, ASP can induce hypersensitivity reactions (HSR) ranging from mild cutaneous manifestations to severe anaphylaxis. Most data on ASP-related hypersensitivity derive from acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), where the reported incidence ranges between 10 and 30% for native E. coli derived ASP and 3-24% for pegylated formulations. However, data on NKTCL remain scarce, even though ASP-containing regimens such as SMILE, LVP, and P-GemOx are increasingly used as frontline or salvage therapies.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: ASP is a bacterial-derived catalytic enzyme available in three main formulations: L-Asparaginase (L-ASP), PEGylated-Asparaginase (PEG-ASP), and crisantaspase (CSP). Both L-ASP and PEG-ASP are derived from Escherichia coli; however, pegylation significantly reduces the immunogenicity of PEG-ASP compared with native L-ASP, resulting in a lower incidence of hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reactions, particularly in patients without prior exposure to native formulations. Crisantaspase, a less immunogenic Erwinia chrysanthemi-derived enzyme, is recommended in these cases to maintain efficacy while avoiding immune hyperreactivity.

Immune-mediated reactions and the development of neutralizing antibodies remain the primary limitations of ASP therapy. These antibodies may occur even in the absence of clinical symptoms, potentially compromising enzymatic activity and treatment efficacy. Nevertheless, evidence on the incidence, clinical features, and management of ASP-related HSRs in NKTCL remains scarce. Systematic evaluation and reporting of these reactions is needed to inform best practices, minimize treatment interruptions, and optimize patient outcomes.
Herein, we report the clinical presentation of an ASP-induced HSR in a patient with NKTCL and present a retrospective institutional review to determine its frequency.
2. Detailed Case Description

A 60-year-old previously healthy female was diagnosed with an ENKTCL-stage EIIA involving the left nasal cavity. She was scheduled to receive "sandwich" therapy consisting of chemotherapy cycles with LVP, followed by radiotherapy and subsequent consolidation with additional cycles of the same chemotherapy regimen. The classical protocol includes two to three cycles of LVP before radiotherapy, radiotherapy at total doses of 50-56 Gy delivered in daily fractions, and two to three additional LVP cycles as consolidation. In Spain, native L-ASP was historically used and imported as a foreign drug. From 2017, PEG-ASP became the preferred formulation due to improved availability and endorsement by cooperative groups such as PETHEMA (Programa Espanol de Tratamientos en Hematologia). Later, in 2023, CSP (Erwinase ) was also introduced to the Spanish market. However, following the discontinuation of L-ASP and the substantially higher cost of CSP, approximately four times that of PEG-ASP, the LVP regimen was adapted to use PEG-ASP at equivalent dosing (PVP).

The chemotherapy regimen consisted of 2500 IU/m2 PEG-ASP administered intravenously on day 1, 1.4 mg/m2 vincristine administered intravenously on day 1, and 100 mg prednisone administered orally on days 1-5, repeated every three weeks. The first PVP cycle was well tolerated, leading to rapid EBV clearance. Radiotherapy was initiated after the first cycle, with 56 Gy administered in 2 Gy daily fractions over 28 sessions, with an integrated boost. The interval between completion of radiotherapy and initiation of the subsequent chemotherapy cycle was extended to eight weeks due to poor tolerance to radiotherapy, which required nasogastric tube placement and enteral nutritional support.

During the second PVP cycle, approximately five minutes after PEG-ASP administration began, she developed palmar erythema, generalized pruritus, marked malaise, sneezing, vomiting, and a presyncopal episode. The infusion was promptly discontinued, and symptoms resolved rapidly following antihistamine and hydrocortisone treatment. She remained afebrile, mildly hypotensive, and eupneic. Due to suspicion of an HSR, additional evaluations were performed by the allergology unit.
Skin Tests for PEG-asparaginase:

The intradermal test (IDT1, 7.5 mg/mL) produced a wheal increase from 3 to 6 mm with 10 mm of erythema and localized pruritus, whereas both skin prick tests (SPT1, 75 mg/mL; SPT2, 750 mg/mL) yielded negative results.
Latency Time (from reaction to skin test): 13 days.
Reaction Biomarkers: Tryptase levels were not drawn at the time of the acute event.
Baseline Tryptase: A baseline tryptase level, drawn during the skin test appointment, was normal.

Based on the ancillary test and the clinical presentation, an immediate (Grade 2, Brown/Grade III, RCUH) hypersensitivity reaction during the infusion of PEG-asparaginase was considered. The skin tests yielded a questionably positive result, but the clinical presentation was consistent with a Type I, IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. However, other immunological mechanisms could not be excluded. The lack of acute-phase biomarker levels (e.g., tryptase) at the time of the event limits etiological confirmation and renders a definitive diagnosis uncertain.

A monitored re-exposure to PEG-asparaginase was attempted. Infusion was stopped after administration of a total dose of 125.42 IU as the patient developed general malaise, epigastric pain, and nausea during the infusion.

Vital signs were initially normal, though she experienced persistent malaise and tachycardia (heart rate 97 bpm). Rapid deterioration prompted treatment with IM epinephrine (0.5 mg), IV dexamethasone (12 mg), and IV dexchlorpheniramine (5 mg). Thirty minutes later, vital signs stabilized, though headache, chest tightness (6/10), and abdominal pain persisted. Intravenous pantoprazole (40 mg) and fluids were administered, leading to gradual recovery within 45 minutes.

The reaction did not meet the criteria for an IgE-mediated reaction, and its lack of improvement with anti-mediator further supported this interpretation. Nevertheless, both events required immediate discontinuation of treatment.
The patient was then switched to CSP, which was well tolerated. The patient remains in complete remission one year after therapy.
3. Retrospective Institutional Review

We retrospectively reviewed data from adult patients (age > 18 years) diagnosed with NK/T-cell lymphoma and treated with ASP-containing chemotherapy regimens between 2015 and 2025 at our institution to determine the frequency of HSR.

This revision was conducted by the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to inclusion. We identified six cases of NKTCL treated with ASP-based chemotherapies from 2015 to 2025. Four patients were of European origin, and the remaining two were of African descent. All patients were treated at the same institution. The median age of the cohort was 52 years (range 42-62), and 67% were male. A total of 94 asparaginase doses were administered (86 native L-ASP, 8 PEG-ASP), with only one documented clinical HSR (1/6, 16.7%).

The treatment regimens administered included SMILE, LVP, P-GemOx, and PVP. A total of 86 intravenous doses of native L-asparaginase were given across these six patients: 6000 IU/m2 on days 1-5 per cycle in the LVP regimen, and on days 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, and 20 in the SMILE regimen. Eight doses of PEG-asparaginase were administered, five intravenously as part of the PVP regimen and three intramuscularly within the P-GemOx protocol. The patient described in our case was the first to receive CSP at our center.
Patients' characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Of the patients treated with ASP-based regimens at our center, only one experienced this reaction.
4. Discussion

Although NK/T-cell lymphoma is a rare hematologic malignancy, its low incidence underscores the need for continued research to better characterize its biological behavior and expand the current understanding of the disease. Such efforts are essential to identify novel pharmacological targets, optimize therapeutic strategies, and develop reliable biomarkers.

Skin testing for L-asparaginase hypersensitivity lacks standardization, as validated diagnostic concentrations have not been established. These tests should therefore be regarded as experimental or complementary rather than definitive and highlight the urgent need for standardization. The same limitation applies to baseline tryptase measurement, which lacks diagnostic value in the absence of corresponding acute-phase levels. In our patient, both assessments were performed for exploratory purposes and were not used as diagnostic criteria.

Hypersensitivity to native and PEG-ASP is influenced by several factors. Thus, studies have shown that adults experience HSRs less frequently than children, and genetic predisposition may contribute to interindividual variability. The use of antihistamines and corticosteroids as premedication has been associated with a reduced incidence of HSRs, and reactions appear less common when ASP is administered as part of intensive chemotherapy regimens with minimal treatment interruptions. In addition, intravenous administration has been linked to a higher rate of anaphylactic reactions compared with intramuscular delivery.

However, managing asparaginase-related immune events is complicated by the cross-reactivity between native L-ASP and PEG-ASP, both E. coli-derived formulations that can induce HSRs. Nevertheless, studies have reported that antibodies against native L-ASP are the most frequently detected (39-61%), while anti-PEG-ASP and anti- CSP antibodies are observed in a less extent (21-29% and 8-38%, respectively). Moreover, individuals producing IgG or IgM anti-ASP antibodies, rather than IgE, are less likely to develop overt hypersensitivity reactions.

Although limited by the sample size, the proportion of patients who developed HSR was very similar to that reported in previous studies. Specifically, in patients diagnosed with ALL or ENKTCL receiving L-ASP, hypersensitivity occurred in 12.5% of cases, a rate comparable to that observed in adult patients who received at least one dose of PEG-ASP in the context of ALL treatment.

In pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the development of antibodies against L-ASP have demonstrated to carry prognostic significance. The presence of specific IgG4 antibodies can predict L-ASP hypersensitivity, while certain chemotherapy regimens, particularly those containing cyclophosphamide, appear to reduce antibody formation, thereby allowing repeated administration of L-ASP without anaphylaxis and preventing the emergence of neutralizing antibodies. Pharmacokinetic studies show that L-ASP has a plasma half-life of 18.3 +- 2.8 h (IV) and 41.7 +- 4.3 h (IM), whereas for CSP the respective values are 7.5 and 15.6 h. PEGylated-ASP, by contrast, exhibits prolonged stability due to PEGylation, with half-lives of 5.73 +- 3.24 days (IM) and 5.29 days (IV), with no significant route-dependent difference.

Importantly, the L-glutaminase coactivity of asparaginase formulations, particularly newer preparations, warrants careful assessment. The measurement of circulating glutamine and glutamate concentrations as surrogate markers of L-glutaminase activity has been proposed as a clinically useful approach, which could be of particular relevance in NKTCL.
5. Conclusions

Similarly to ALL, HSRs remain a major challenge in the treatment of NK/T-cell lymphoma with asparaginase, compromising both safety and efficacy. It is crucial to properly distinguish between the immune-mediated toxicities associated with ASP formulations, to assess their impact on this disease, and to establish appropriate management strategies based on clinical findings, available analytical tests, and any existing reference values. Establishing standardized diagnostic and grading criteria supported by clinical and laboratory evidence is critical to achieve consistent evaluation and improve patient management.
